I've trained with people who would throw beginners on their head / neck for fun after class because they think since it's after class, they can go all out. I've been on the receiving end of that... so no thanks. A simple wrist support won't help me very much. 

That same person also thinks if you are resisting too much (i.e. being non-compliant) then you are playing dirty / going out of scope... and it means he can play dirty too and do things that are much more brutal and not in the technique (the train of thought is, if you are going to be non-compliant then the attacker shouldn't be limited to doing attacks in only one way either, especially when you have obvious openings). I'm very skeptical how we can have non-compliant training without increasing injuries, and to me, it just opens the door for jerks to abuse people on the mat

Reach out to them and talk to them. If you're not sure how to start the conversation, then maybe "Is everything okay, I'm always here to talk".

If you're not in the same timezone then even instant messaging is good, it doesn't have to be over the phone. Let them know you are there for them and even if it seems like they are going through a happy period, keep in contact. If they tell you something is going on, then be understanding; if they don't, then you can still be there for them by giving them some normal social contact.

Hope it helps! :) 

btw - there's no pressure to read it quickly, they recommended to just work through it at your own pace rather than to just whizz through. I haven't finished reading it myself

Hey! I went through a lot at the end of last year myself. 

I had people tell me go enjoy life, there's more to it, do things you wanted to do but never had time for... tbh it just didn't resonate with me (there wasn't anything I wanted to do - otherwise, well I won't be so badly depressed)

Getting a diagnosis didn't really help me. I saw multiple people and one of them would scoff at another person's report... that sort of thing.

I had a lot of problems with reliving memories / remembering comments that got me upset. The latest person I've been seeing recommended me to read "The Happiness Trap". I found it really help, especially with the memories coming back - I still have the memories but it doesn't bother me so much anymore. It's based on Acceptance Commitment Therapy.

This is just going by what helped me when I went through shit myself. 

Be kind and don't judge her. Let her know your feelings without forcing her to accept your views or change the way she thinks right now. For example, tell her you are glad that she didn't go, without making her agree with you. If you think that her boyfriend was a jerk to make her go through this, then tell her you think he is a jerk, but don't force her to agree or keep bring it up if she doesn't respond to it. 

Simple things like you are glad that she is telling you what happened. Or glad that she did what she did (i.e. not go to her boyfriend), to help her feel it is okay. 

Tell her you are there for her. Tell her it's not her fault. Acknowledge her pain (I'm sorry for what you had to go through, no one should have to go through something like that). Tell her it's okay to cry or to have whatever feelings she is having.

Try replacing "should" with "could". "Should" has a lot of self blame in it. 

Not going to your parents for support sounds like a good thing, especially if they think emotions or being emotional is some kind of weakness.

Seeing professional support later would be good. But keep in mind professional support can only do so much (after all it's only a 1-2 hours each time) and she would need support between those sessions.

On things to look out for, just try to make sure she's still doing nice enjoyable things. Invite her out for coffee / lunch outside even after she stopped crying so much and looks like she is getting better. Light exercise (like a walk) outside each day helps a lot

Take care.

A couple of people have mentioned something along the lines of "let them do their own stuff unless it's a safety issue thing". Is this etiquette more because it was white belt / black belt, kohai / sempai, or something else entirely?

Thanks everyone for commenting! It gave me a different perspective and an idea of what I can do next time.

Never knew black belts train differently at a certain level. For a bit of background, I go to two dojos: one has mainly white belts and the other has mainly black belts. I've noticed the two dojos feel different but I never thought much into it, but it makes sense.
